page: Microsoft Azure E8as_v6 is a memory-optimized virtual machine belonging to the Eav6 family, running on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. It features 8 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 4 physical AMD EPYC 9V74 cores with multithreading enabled. The CPU operates at a base frequency of 3.7 GHz and includes 32 MB of L3 cache. The instance is equipped with 64.0 GB of system memory, yielding a high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8.0 GB per core. It does not include local storage or bundled GPUs, though it is Premium Storage capable.

Performance benchmarks show strong single-core capabilities, with stress-ng single-core and Geekbench single-core scores placing in the top 25%. Multi-core performance, including stress-ng multi-core and Geekbench multi-core, falls within the average range. Memory performance is mixed; while cached small-block read bandwidth is average at 608.08 GB/sec, uncached large-block read bandwidth is weak at 38.21 GB/sec. Text processing and single-threaded decompression tasks perform well, whereas medium-sized LLM prompt processing using a 7B model is weak at 23.47 tokens/sec.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the E8as_v6 provides a high-density memory allocation relative to its compute footprint, making it a viable option for memory-bound workloads without paying for excess vCPUs. The lack of local storage requires external block storage attachment. This server is suited for memory-intensive applications such as relational databases, caching layers like Redis, data processing, and general-purpose enterprise workloads that require a 1:8 vCPU-to-RAM ratio.
description: The Microsoft Azure E8as_v6 is an x86_64 memory-optimized virtual machine from the Eav6 family, powered by an AMD EPYC 9V74 processor running at 3.7 GHz. It features 8 dedicated vCPUs (4 physical cores with multithreading) and 64.0 GB of RAM, establishing a high 1:8 vCPU-to-memory ratio. The instance does not include local storage or integrated GPUs but is Premium Storage capable. Benchmarks indicate strong single-core CPU and text processing performance, while multi-core execution and database operations remain average. A notable performance tradeoff is its weak uncached large-block memory read bandwidth of 38.21 GB/sec and slow 7B LLM prompt processing. This configuration is qualitatively cost-efficient for memory-heavy workloads that do not require massive parallel compute, making it well-suited for relational databases, Redis caching, and memory-intensive enterprise applications.
